verdicts.trueWording: when the model is apparently the most certain... it is most overconfident
verdicts.note: Quote verbatim in Section 3 ('Dependency of the confidence on the entropy'). Both limbs hold: 'the level of overconfidence decreases with the entropy percentile', and the paper's own note that at low entropy a single token's probability can exceed 0.9, so the top-p set is at its narrowest and cannot be recalibrated by resizing. 10 entropy bins by percentile, Fig. 3, as the page field says.

verdicts.trueWording: calibration shows a moderate inverse scaling with model size
verdicts.note: Quote verbatim in the abstract; Section 3 'Calibration and scale' restates it as calibration deteriorating moderately with model scale (Fig. 4, threshold q-hat above the y=x line for every confidence level, i.e. overconfident throughout). Metadata nit only, not a claim limb: Fig. 4 plots 125M, 350M, 1B, 2B, 6B, 13B, 30B, not the '1.3B' listed in modelEra.

verdicts.unsupportedLimb: 'one of the few decoding studies to work in the encyclopedic register' - the paper makes no comparative claim about other decoding studies' registers
verdicts.trueWording: We ran the models on 10,000 English Wikipedia predictions
verdicts.note: First limb verbatim and exact (Section 3 Setup, HuggingFace wikipedia dataset); note the paper counts 10,000 *predictions* across entropy percentiles, not 10,000 documents or 'items'. The comparative second limb is the verifier's or the register-hint's framing, absent from the page. Separately, generation quality (MAUVE/BERTScore) was measured on OpenWebText prompts, not Wikipedia.

verdicts.trueWording: Larger nucleus sizes only modestly mitigate memorization
verdicts.note: Quote verbatim in abstract point (i); Conclusion repeats it. 'Verbatim' is fair: the paper's memorization metric is Carlini et al.'s exact-string reproduction f(p)=s, contrasted with 'soft' memorization. Two fine-tuned GPT-Neo models = 125M and 350M. Caveat worth carrying: the effect is uneven - larger top_p helps substantially at duplicate 'ramp-up points' and barely at saturation (Finding 2).

verdicts.trueWording: outputs that echo the training data but without a complete one-by-one resemblance
verdicts.note: Quote verbatim in the abstract; the 'survives nucleus sampling' limb is carried by the Conclusion, which says that even when outputs are not exact reproductions, 'n-gram overlap scores indicate a soft memorization' phenomenon, and by Table 2, where BLEU-4 for non-verbatim outputs stays high at top_p 0.8 (0.67-0.73 at high duplicate counts). Their stated cause: peaked distributions where one token exceeds the nucleus threshold, making sampling deterministic.

verdicts.trueWording: extracts the dynamic patterns (spectrum) of text surprisal
verdicts.note: No quote was supplied, so graded on substance. Abstract defines FACE-2 as a psycholinguistically inspired metric extracting the dynamic patterns (spectrum) of surprisal; Section 2.1 grounds surprisal over 'time (or, the position in body of text)'; the abstract closes by advocating metrics that mine the dynamics of likelihood - i.e. against a static score. Registers confirmed: five English sets (Wikipedia, BBC-News, WritingPrompts and two QA sets) plus three Chinese.

verdicts.trueWording: larger models produce spectrum (blue and purple) that resembles human (red) more
verdicts.note: Quote verbatim in the Figure 5 caption, which is exactly the GAM-smoothed spectrum plots the claim describes. Scope note: the caption calls these exemplars and frames it as FACE-2 revealing 'the expected order' where FACE-1 does not, so the finding is about the metric's sensitivity as much as about the models.

verdicts.trueWording: original conclusions on modeling scaling effects and sampling methods does not necessarily
verdicts.note: Quote verbatim in Section 2.1, in the list of FACE-1 limitations: FACE-1 is 'developed and tested using GPT-2' data, so its 'original conclusions on modeling scaling effects' need not apply to current LLMs (the paper's own agreement slip, 'does not', preserved). Every limb - Fourier-of-surprisal predecessor, GPT-2 provenance, scaling and sampling conclusions, current LLMs - is on the page.

verdicts.trueWording: more advanced sampling method... have a better FACE-2 scores
verdicts.note: Quote verbatim in Section 4.2 'Comparison with sampling methods'; Appendix B.1 Table 5 carries the numbers. Two cautions for any downstream use: the margins are small and one setting is a tie (SO 0.58 nucleus p=0.95 vs 0.57 pure sampling and top-k 40; greedy is the clear loser at 0.55 / EMD 6.43), and Table 5 is a single cell - generator Gemma2-2b-base, inference Llama3-70b-base, BBC data - not the Qwen2/Llama3 sweep named in modelEra.

verdicts.trueWording: optimal configurations vary across models and tasks
verdicts.note: Quote verbatim in the abstract; the 2.2 million continuations are contribution 4 in Section 1, and Section 6 works the model-by-model and dataset-by-dataset recommendations out in detail. 'No single configuration best everywhere' is the fair reading of 'vary across models and tasks'.

verdicts.trueWording: Larger models do not show a clear advantage over smaller ones
verdicts.note: Quote verbatim, and the GPT2-XL/Llama3 limb is explicit twice in Section 6: under temperature, 'GPT2-XL (1.5B) might outperform Llama3 (8B)' at the same configuration; under top-k, GPT2-XL 'performs as well as or better than' Llama3 8B, with Qwen2 7B over Falcon2 11B. Location correction for the page field: Section 6 Practical Recommendations, not Section 5.

verdicts.trueWording: consistently low performance across all models and beam width settings
verdicts.note: Quote verbatim in Section 6, 'Deterministic Strategies', which cites Figure 4 as the claim's page field says: beam search is 'generally not recommended for open-ended text generation' because its outputs fail to capture human diversity, showing low performance against human references on four metrics. The paper does add that smaller beam widths (3, 5) fare better while still leaving a substantial gap - a nuance, not a contradiction.

verdicts.trueWording: In total, we generate 2.2 million text continuations, which are publicly available
verdicts.note: Quote verbatim in Section 1, contribution 4, with the release URL. 'Automatic metrics alongside human judgments' mirrors the abstract's own wording. Scope caveat for downstream use: the human component is 570 evaluations (Table 3, Pearson r = 0.64), a sample of the 2.2M corpus, not a human rating of every continuation.

verdicts.unsupportedLimb: 'behaviourally identical' - the paper says 'behaviorally similar' and 'superficially similar', and Section 5 measures a behavioural difference between the two (natural repetition starts at higher, wider-spread entropy; ICL converges to near-zero entropy by cycle 4)
verdicts.trueWording: Repetition in this condition lacks a clearly identifiable circuit
verdicts.note: Quote verbatim in the Discussion. The substantive limbs all hold: ICL repetition 'relies on a dedicated network of attention heads' that specialise over training, while natural repetition 'emerges early and lacks a defined circuitry'. Only the strength word fails - swap 'behaviourally identical' for 'superficially similar' and this becomes verbatim-clean.

verdicts.trueWording: natural repetition focuses disproportionately on low-information tokens, suggesting a fallback behavior
verdicts.note: Quote verbatim in the abstract, continuing '...when relevant context cannot be retrieved'. Section 4.2 supplies the numbers (newline tokens attended 9.9x uniform expectation under natural prompts vs 3.1x under ICL) and the Discussion names 'punctuation or syntactic markers'. Important adjacent finding the claim does not distort but a reader should know: causal tests (adding, removing, reweighting newlines) produced zero change, so the attention pattern co-occurs with repetition rather than causing it.
